claim: Recordings were made from ensembles of place cells in 4 rats with 37-66 place cells each, totaling 212 cells.
source: To this end, we recorded from ensembles of place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971) (4 rats, 37–66 place cells each, 212 cells in total) while rats ran along a T-shaped track (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 1) with visible yet inaccessible arms (Figure 1A)—RUN1.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of animals, cells per animal, and total cells recorded.

claim: Spiking events were defined as periods of 300 ms or less where at least 15% of cells were active.
source: During a rest period before RUN1 (REST1) and after GOAL-CUE (REST2), spiking events—periods of 300 ms or less, where at least 15% of cells were active (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsaki, 2007)—were analysed.
evidence: The manuscript provides the operational definition of spiking events with citation support.

claim: Spiking events were associated with significantly higher power in the ripple spectrum (80-250 Hz) than other comparable periods.
source: These spiking events were associated with significantly higher power in the ripple spectrum (80–250 Hz) than other comparable periods (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure showing the data.

claim: All four animals displayed more interest in the cued arm than the uncued arm during GOAL-CUE, with a mean bias of 0.33 based on dwell time.
source: During GOAL-CUE, all four animals displayed more interest in the cued arm than the uncued arm (as indexed by the difference in time spent on the cued side of the stem vs the uncued side, divided by the total time spent on either side, mean bias = 0.33).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral measurements showing preferential attention to the cued arm.

claim: Prior to goal-cueing, two animals spent more time on the uncued side of the stem with a mean bias of 0.10.
source: In contrast, prior to goal-cueing, two animals spent more time on the uncued side of the stem (mean bias = 0.10, see Table 1 for results for individual animals).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data from the pre-cueing period.

claim: During GOAL-CUE all animals spent more time looking towards the cued arm than the uncued arm with a mean bias of 0.13.
source: Moreover, during GOAL-CUE all animals also spent more time looking towards the cued arm than the uncued arm (mean bias = 0.13), again this bias was not observed prior to goal-cueing when only one animal spent more time looking towards the cued arm (mean bias = −0.11, see Table 1 for results of individual animals).
evidence: The manuscript reports head direction measurements showing preferential orientation toward the cued arm.

claim: During RUN2 when the barrier was first removed, all four animals initially turned towards the cued arm with a mean bias of 0.96.
source: Furthermore, during RUN2 when the barrier was first removed and the food cue was no longer present, all four animals initially turned towards the cued arm and spent more time on the cued rather than the uncued arm (mean bias = 0.96, see Table 1 for results for individual animals).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral preference data from the exploration phase.

claim: In REST2, there was significant preplay of the yet unvisited cued arm at 7.37% of events (p < 0.001).
source: Consistent with the behavioural bias, in REST2 we found significant preplay of the yet unvisited cued arm (7.37% preplay events, p < 0.001, binomial test vs chance, Figure 2A,D).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of preplay events with p-value and references supporting figures.

claim: The uncued arm was not significantly preplayed in REST2 (4.41% preplay events, p = 0.33).
source: Conversely, the uncued arm was not significantly preplayed (4.41% preplay events p = 0.33, vs cued arm: p < 0.001, Figure 2B,D).
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of significant preplay for the uncued arm with statistical comparison.

claim: Significant effects of preplay were found when animals were analysed individually.
source: Similarly significant effects were found when animals were analysed individually (see Figure 2D, Table 2), although the results for one animal were based on a relatively small sample (number of cued preplay events = 9, R1838), it still showed significant preplay of the cued arm.
evidence: The manuscript reports that individual animal analyses confirmed the group-level findings.

claim: The area under the curve (AUC) analysis corroborated the preplay findings, showing significant preplay for the cued arm (p < 0.001) but not the uncued arm (p = 0.22).
source: Moreover, the results were corroborated by a distribution-based analysis; namely, comparing the area under the curve (AUC) of bootstrapped cumulative distributions of absolute correlations for each arm to that of their shuffle distribution (Figure 2A,B, cued: p < 0.001, uncued: p = 0.22, cued vs uncued: p = 0.0044, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports an alternative statistical analysis confirming the main findings.

claim: Preplay events of the cued arm were equally likely to represent paths to and from the cued arm (7.34% vs 7.40%, p = 0.49).
source: Preplay events of the cued arm were equally likely to represent paths to and from the cued arm (7.34% vs 7.40% p = 0.49) and to run towards ('forward') and away ('reverse') from the ends of the arms (6.93% vs 7.80%, p = 0.18, Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports directional analysis of preplay sequences with statistical comparisons.

claim: Preplay events were equally likely to run towards ('forward') and away ('reverse') from the ends of the arms (6.93% vs 7.80%, p = 0.18).
source: Preplay events of the cued arm were equally likely to represent paths to and from the cued arm (7.34% vs 7.40% p = 0.49) and to run towards ('forward') and away ('reverse') from the ends of the arms (6.93% vs 7.80%, p = 0.18, Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports bidirectional preplay with statistical comparison.

claim: The amount of preplay exhibited by each animal appeared to be predicted by the interest they displayed for the cued arm during GOAL-CUE.
source: Moreover, the amount of preplay exhibited by each animal appeared to be predicted by the interest they displayed for the cued arm during GOAL-CUE (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports a correlation between behavioral interest and preplay magnitude.

claim: Preferential preplay of the cued arm could not be explained by differences in the number of cells with fields on the arms.
source: Importantly, preferential preplay of the cued arm could not be explained by differences in the number of cells with fields on the arms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B), spike-sorting quality (cells with neighbouring place fields were as well separated in cluster-space as those with distant fields, p = 0.45, 2-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test), place field stability on the two arms (cued arm stability r = 0.54 vs uncued arm stability r = 0.49, p = 0.15) or the location of place fields on the cued arm (Figure 3B, p = 0.22 two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: The manuscript reports multiple control analyses ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: Cells with neighbouring place fields were as well separated in cluster-space as those with distant fields (p = 0.45).
source: Importantly, preferential preplay of the cued arm could not be explained by differences in the number of cells with fields on the arms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B), spike-sorting quality (cells with neighbouring place fields were as well separated in cluster-space as those with distant fields, p = 0.45, 2-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test), place field stability on the two arms (cued arm stability r = 0.54 vs uncued arm stability r = 0.49, p = 0.15) or the location of place fields on the cued arm (Figure 3B, p = 0.22 two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: The manuscript reports cluster quality analysis to rule out spike-sorting artifacts.

claim: Place field stability did not differ significantly between cued and uncued arms (cued r = 0.54 vs uncued r = 0.49, p = 0.15).
source: Importantly, preferential preplay of the cued arm could not be explained by differences in the number of cells with fields on the arms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B), spike-sorting quality (cells with neighbouring place fields were as well separated in cluster-space as those with distant fields, p = 0.45, 2-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test), place field stability on the two arms (cued arm stability r = 0.54 vs uncued arm stability r = 0.49, p = 0.15) or the location of place fields on the cued arm (Figure 3B, p = 0.22 two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: The manuscript reports place field stability measurements to rule out differential stability as an explanation.

claim: Preplay of the cued arm was higher in REST2 than REST1 (7.37% vs 4.74%, p < 0.001).
source: Preplay of the cued arm was higher in REST2 than REST1 (7.37% vs 4.74%, p < 0.001, Figure 2C,E), an effect that was seen for all animals (Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal comparison showing preplay increases after goal-cueing.

claim: The cued arm was not significantly preplayed during REST1 (4.74%, p = 0.34).
source: Indeed, the cued arm was not significantly preplayed during REST1 (4.74%, p = 0.34).
evidence: The manuscript reports lack of preplay before goal-cueing.

claim: Preplay of the stem was not found during REST1 (4.12% preplay events, p = 0.44).
source: We did not find preplay of the stem (4.12% preplay events, p = 0.44, AUC analysis p = 0.053, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Table 3, RUN1 REST1 vs cued REST2: p < 0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of stem preplay to address temporal delay concerns.

claim: Based on AUC analysis, the cued but not the uncued arm was preplayed during GOAL-CUE (p = 0.02, p = 0.24 respectively).
source: However, based on a bootstrapped comparison of the AUC for absolute correlations from the cued and uncued arm vs shuffled distributions, we found that the cued but not the uncued arm was preplayed (p = 0.02, p = 0.24 respectively, Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports preplay analysis during the goal-cueing period itself.

claim: Direct comparison of the proportion of preplay events for the cued vs uncued arm during GOAL-CUE was marginally not significant (6.4% vs 4.12%, p = 0.052).
source: A direct comparison of the proportion of preplay events for the cued vs uncued arm was marginally not significant (6.4% vs 4.12%, p = 0.052, see Table 4 for results for individual animals).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical comparison that approached but did not reach significance.

claim: During REST1 and RUN1, future cued and uncued arm cells did not differ in activity for both the first and second half of these periods.
source: During REST1 and RUN1 the future cued and uncued arm cells did not differ in activity, this was true for both the first and second half of these periods (mean cued/uncued rate ratio: REST1 early ratio = 0.96, p = 0.88, REST1 late ratio = 1.04 p = 0.09, RUN1 early ratio = 1.09 p = 0.32, RUN1 late ratio = 1.18 p = 0.22, Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal evolution analysis of cell activity.

claim: During GOAL-CUE, cued arm cells were significantly more active than uncued arm cells, with the effect most pronounced during the first half (early ratio = 1.78, p = 0.01; late = 1.46, p < 0.01).
source: However, during GOAL-CUE cued arm cells were significantly more active than uncued arm cells, an effect that was most pronounced during the first half (5 min) of the cueing period (GOAL-CUE early ratio = 1.78, p = 0.01, late = 1.46, p < 0.01).
evidence: The manuscript reports differential cell activity during goal-cueing with temporal resolution.

claim: The difference between cued and uncued arm cell activity persisted through REST2, albeit attenuating with time (early ratio = 1.30, p < 0.001; late ratio = 1.10, p < 0.01).
source: Finally, the difference between the two groups persisted through the subsequent rest period, albeit attenuating with time (REST2 early ratio = 1.30 p < 0.001, REST2 late ratio = 1.10 p < 0.01, Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports persistence of differential activity into the rest period.

claim: The bias in sequential preplay is not a mere product of differing activity levels of the cells for the two arms.
source: Importantly, control analyses showed that the bias in sequential preplay is not a mere product of differing activity levels of the cells for the two arms (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: The manuscript reports control analyses ruling out activity rate as the sole explanation.

claim: Biased pre-activation of future experiences is instantiated at the point when an environment becomes motivationally-relevant.
source: Together, these findings indicate that biased pre-activation of future experiences is instantiated at the point when an environment becomes motivationally-relevant.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the temporal evolution of preplay bias.

claim: Using Bayesian reconstruction analysis, during REST2, preplay of the cued arm was found (7.64% of events, p < 0.001) but not of the uncued arm (4.78% of events, p = 0.55).
source: Again, during REST2, we found preplay of the cued arm (7.64% of events, p < 0.001, binomial test) but not of the uncued arm (4.78% of events, p = 0.55, vs cued = p < 0.001, Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript reports an alternative analysis method confirming the main findings.

claim: Using Bayesian reconstruction, neither the cued nor the uncued arm were significantly preplayed in REST1 (cued = 5.04%, p = 0.43; uncued = 4.69%, p = 0.55).
source: Moreover, neither the cued nor the uncued arm were significantly preplayed in REST1 (cued = 5.04%, p = 0.43, uncued = 4.69%, p = 0.55, Figure 4F).
evidence: The manuscript reports Bayesian analysis results for the pre-cueing rest period.

claim: The Bayesian decoder performed equally well on the cued and uncued arms with a median error of 10.0 cm for both arms.
source: The Bayesian decoder performed equally well on the cued and uncued arms (Figure 4A,B, median error for both arms = 10.0 cm).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation of the decoding method.

claim: Preplay events were found to exhibit higher power in the ripple spectrum than non-significant spiking events.
source: These preplay events were found to exhibit higher power in the ripple spectrum than non-significant spiking events (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports physiological characteristics of preplay events.

claim: Preplay of a visible, unvisited environment that has motivational relevance accords with reports indicating a crucial role for the hippocampus in processing future goals.
source: Preplay of a visible, unvisited environment that has motivational relevance to an animal accords with various reports from neuropsychological and imaging studies indicating a crucial role for the hippocampus in processing future goals (Spiers and Barry, 2015), imagination, and future thinking (Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript relates findings to prior literature on hippocampal function.

claim: These findings agree with previous studies showing replay can be modulated by reward but extend this modulatory influence to preplay of future, goal-oriented routes.
source: Moreover, these findings agree with previous studies showing replay can be modulated by reward (Cheng and Frank, 2008; Singer and Frank, 2009; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013) but extend this modulatory influence to preplay of future, goal-oriented routes.
evidence: The manuscript contextualizes findings within existing reward-modulation literature.

claim: Replay of sequences leading towards goal locations has previously been linked with the planning of future trajectories.
source: Replay of sequences leading towards goal locations has previously been linked with the planning of future trajectories (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on forward replay and planning.

claim: The elevated proportion of preplay events leading to the cued goal might reflect route planning, given the animals' subsequent preference for the cued arm.
source: Plausibly the elevated proportion of preplay events we observed leading to the cued goal might also reflect route planning—especially given the animals' subsequent preference for the cued arm.
evidence: The manuscript offers an interpretation of forward preplay based on behavioral outcomes.

claim: Reverse replay has often been characterised as a solution to the temporal credit assignment problem, providing a learning mechanism to evaluate a sequence of actions that led to a successful outcome.
source: However, reverse replay has often been characterised as a solution to the temporal credit assignment problem (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Foster and Knierim, 2012)—providing a learning mechanism to evaluate a sequence of actions that led to a successful outcome.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior theoretical work on reverse replay function.

claim: An intriguing possibility is that paths towards the goal might be simulated using forwards preplay then evaluated and learnt from during reverse preplay.
source: In the context of preplay, when the cued arm has not been physically visited, an intriguing possibility is that paths towards the goal might be simulated using forwards preplay then evaluated and learnt from during reverse preplay, in a manner similar to that proposed to exist for periods of exploration and post-exploration rest (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Buhry et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a speculative mechanism for bidirectional preplay.

claim: Several studies have described 'de novo preplay'—preplay of environments that have yet to be experienced—which is believed to reflect the activity of preconfigured cell ensembles.
source: Recently several studies have described 'de novo preplay'—preplay of environments that have yet to be experienced (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011, 2013, 2013)—which is believed to reflect the activity of preconfigured cell ensembles (McNaughton et al., 1996) that subsequently become bound to sensory cues in the environment.
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on de novo preplay and its theoretical basis.

claim: De novo preplay was not observed in the current experiment (no preplay of stem during REST1).
source: We did not observe de novo preplay in the current experiment (no preplay of stem during REST1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of de novo preplay.

claim: Several other studies also do not find de novo preplay for a completely novel environment.
source: Although the origin of this discrepancy is unclear, we note that several other studies also do not find de novo preplay for a completely novel environment (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Lee and Wilson, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies with similar negative findings.

claim: Environmental factors such as the barrier and visible but inaccessible arms might have ameliorated de novo preplay.
source: However, it seems likely that other environmental factors present here but absent in the do novo preplay studies (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011, 2013, 2014), such as the barrier, and visible but inaccessible arms, might have ameliorated this phenomenon.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on methodological differences affecting de novo preplay.

claim: The AUC analysis comparing spiking events during REST1 against the stem template was narrowly not significant (p = 0.053).
source: Indeed, the AUC analysis comparing spiking events recorded during REST1 against the stem template (RUN1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) was narrowly not significant (p = 0.053), suggesting that perhaps with more data or a simpler environment we might have found de novo preplay for the stem.
evidence: The manuscript reports a marginally non-significant result suggesting possible de novo preplay.

claim: The complexity of the environment might have worked against observing a background rate of de novo preplay for the uncued arm during REST2.
source: In a similar vein one might also have expected to observe a background rate of de novo preplay for the uncued arm during REST2. Again it seems possible that the complexity of the environment worked against such an effect in that the motivationally relevant cued arm was preplayed at the expense of the uncued arm.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on why de novo preplay was not observed for the uncued arm.

claim: It remains to be understood if the bias in preplay reflects an active process simulating trajectories associated with the goal, or if the relevance of the cued arm simply allows it to more effectively capture preconfigured cell assemblies.
source: What remains to be understood is if this bias reflects an active process, simulating trajectories associated with the goal, or if the relevance of the cued arm simply allows it to more effectively capture preconfigured cell assemblies.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges uncertainty about the underlying mechanism.

claim: The data indicates that preplay of an unvisited environment can be initiated in response to viewing that environment if it is relevant to future goals.
source: In sum, our data indicates that preplay of an unvisited environment can be initiated in response to viewing that environment if it is relevant to future goals—features that were absent in previous studies investigating the formation of hippocampal representations for novel spaces (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Lee and Wilson, 2002; Rowland et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding and contrasts it with prior work.

claim: The data does not provide direct support for de novo preplay but also does not argue against it.
source: Furthermore, although our data does not provide direct support for de novo preplay it also does not argue against it, and is consistent with the hypothesis that the hippocampus supports the construction of novel spatial experiences as suggested by other authors (for example see Dragoi and Tonegawa (2014)).
evidence: The manuscript clarifies the relationship between findings and de novo preplay theory.

claim: The results are consistent with the notion that place cells form preconfigured assemblies or 'charts'.
source: These results are consistent with the notion that place cells form preconfigured assemblies or 'charts' (McNaughton et al., 1996)—an active but unassigned chart being associated with the cued arm during GOAL-CUE, but do not preclude the possibility that place cell firing is driven in a feed-forward manner (e.g., Hartley et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript relates findings to theoretical frameworks about place cell organization.

claim: These findings support the hypothesised role of preplay for preparation for future experiences but extend it to simulating future experiences in environments yet to be actively explored.
source: We conclude that these findings support the hypothesised role of preplay for preparation for future experiences (Diba and Buzsaki, 2007; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Foster and Knierim, 2012; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013) but extend it to simulating future experiences in environments yet to be actively explored.
evidence: The manuscript states the main conclusion relating findings to prior theoretical work.

claim: It remains to be seen if the ability of the hippocampus to construct future spatial sequences is related to the generation of more abstract temporal associations.
source: It remains to be seen if the ability of the hippocampus to construct future spatial sequences is related to the generation of more abstract temporal associations (Kraus et al., 2013; Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript poses an open question about broader implications.

claim: Four male lister-hooded rats were used in this study.
source: Four male lister-hooded rats were used in this study.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental subjects.

claim: All procedures were approved by the UK Home Office, subject to the restrictions and provisions contained in the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act of 1986.
source: All procedures were approved by the UK Home Office, subject to the restrictions and provisions contained in the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act of 1986.
evidence: The manuscript states ethical approval for the study.

claim: Two rats received two microdrives, each carrying four tetrodes, targeted to the left and right CA1.
source: Two rats (330–333 g at implantation) received two microdrives, each carrying four tetrodes of twisted 25 µm HM-L coated platinum iridium wire (90% and 10%, respectively; California Fine Wire), targeted to the left and right CA1.
evidence: The manuscript describes the surgical implantation procedure.

claim: One animal received a single microdrive carrying eight tetrodes targeting right CA1.
source: One animal (350 g) received a single microdrive, carrying eight tetrodes, targeting right CA1.
evidence: The manuscript describes the surgical implantation for one animal.

claim: One animal received one microdrive carrying four tetrodes targeting the mEC and one carrying four tetrodes targeting contralateral CA1, with only CA1 units included in the study.
source: Finally, one animal (425 g) received one microdrive carrying four tetrodes of 12- µm wire targeted to the mEC and one carrying four tetrodes of 17- µm wire targeted to contralateral CA1. Only single units from the CA1 implant were included in this study.
evidence: The manuscript describes the surgical implantation and data selection for one animal.

claim: The T-shaped track consisted of 10 cm wide runways covered in black rubber, with a stem 222 cm long and arms 200 cm from tip to tip.
source: We used a T-shaped track, raised 43 cm off the ground. The track consisted of 10 cm wide runways covered in black rubber, the stem was 222 cm long and the arms 200 cm from tip to tip.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental apparatus dimensions.

claim: A barrier was placed on the stem 22 cm from the junction with the arms to prevent animals from accessing the arms.
source: Initially, to prevent animals from accessing the arms, a barrier was placed on the stem 22 cm from the junction with the arms.
evidence: The manuscript describes the barrier placement in the experimental setup.

claim: The barrier consisted of a grill of vertical wooden bars spaced so the animals could easily see through but could not scale it.
source: The barrier consisted of a grill of vertical wooden bars spaced so the animals could easily see through but could not scale it.
evidence: The manuscript describes the barrier design allowing visual access.

claim: Textured local cues were placed along the stem and arms to encourage even distribution of place fields.
source: To encourage even distribution of place fields along the track, textured local cues were placed along the stem and arms.
evidence: The manuscript describes environmental enrichment for place field distribution.

claim: Five different textured cues were used: black rubber, grey cardboard, black polypropylene, plaster tape, and sandpaper, each approximately 20 cm long and 10 cm wide.
source: These five different cues were sheets of: black rubber, grey cardboard, black polypropylene, plaster tape, and sandpaper each approximately 20 cm long and 10 cm wide.
evidence: The manuscript describes the specific cues used in the environment.

claim: Ratemaps for the runs on the arms during RUN2 were generated after removing the last 20 cm of each arm and excluding position samples where the animal's speed was lower than 3 cm/s.
source: Ratemaps for the runs on the arms during RUN2 were generated. Prior to ratemap generation, the last 20 cm (10%) of each arm were removed to exclude areas where the animal groomed, ate etc. Similarly, to avoid non-perambulatory behaviours, position samples where the animal's speed was lower than 3 cm/s were excluded.
evidence: The manuscript describes data preprocessing for ratemap generation.

claim: Cells whose peak firing rate in the linearised ratemap were below 0.5 Hz, had less than five contiguous bins with rates above the mean firing rate, or whose spatial correlation between the first and second half of RUN2 was less than 0.3 were excluded.
source: Cells whose peak firing rate in the linearised ratemap were below 0.5 Hz, had less than five contiguous bins with rates above the mean firing rate of the cell, or whose spatial correlation between the first and second half of the RUN2 session was less than 0.3 were excluded.
evidence: The manuscript describes cell inclusion criteria for analysis.

claim: Preplay events were identified as those with either a significant positive or negative correlation using a two-tailed test, each tail tested at the 97.5% level.
source: Preplay events were identified as those with either a significant positive or negative correlation—a two-tailed test, each tail tested at the 97.5% level.
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical criteria for identifying preplay events.

claim: To establish significance at the population level, the proportion of preplay events measured was compared to a null distribution generated by calculating correlations between place cell templates and shuffled sequences from events.
source: To establish significance at the population level, the proportion of preplay events measured was compared to a null distribution generated by calculating correlations between place cell templates and shuffled sequences from events (see Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical approach for population-level significance.

claim: The sequence of spikes in each event was randomly permuted 100 times by randomly re-assigning cell IDs such that spikes from the same cell were never separated.
source: Next, the sequence of spikes in each event was randomly permuted (shuffled) 100 times by randomly re-assigning cell IDs such that spikes from the same cell were never separated.
evidence: The manuscript describes the shuffling procedure for generating null distributions.

claim: LFP from CA1 was recorded at 4.8 kHz throughout the experiment.
source: LFP from CA1 was recorded at 4.8 kHz throughout the experiment.
evidence: The manuscript describes the local field potential recording parameters.

claim: To analyse sharp-wave ripples, the LFP was band-pass filtered between 80 and 250 Hz.
source: To analyse sharp-wave ripples (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Buzsaki et al., 1992) the LFP was band-pass filtered between 80 and 250 Hz.
evidence: The manuscript describes the signal processing for ripple analysis.

claim: Viewing the delivery of food to an unvisited portion of an environment leads to off-line pre-activation of place cell sequences corresponding to that space.
source: Here we report that viewing the delivery of food to an unvisited portion of an environment leads to off-line pre-activation of place cells sequences corresponding to that space.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Preplay was not observed for an unrewarded but otherwise similar portion of the environment.
source: Such 'preplay' was not observed for an unrewarded but otherwise similar portion of the environment.
evidence: This is a key negative control finding stated in the abstract.

claim: A hippocampal representation of a visible, yet unexplored environment can be formed if the environment is of motivational relevance to the animal.
source: These results suggest that a hippocampal representation of a visible, yet unexplored environment can be formed if the environment is of motivational relevance to the animal.
evidence: This is the main interpretation stated in the abstract.

claim: Goal-biased preplay may support preparation for future experiences in novel environments.
source: We hypothesise such goal-biased preplay may support preparation for future experiences in novel environments.
evidence: This is the hypothesized functional role stated in the abstract.

claim: Dominant theories of hippocampal function propose that place cell representations are formed during an animal's first encounter with a novel environment and are subsequently replayed during off-line states to support consolidation and future behaviour.
source: Dominant theories of hippocampal function propose that place cell representations are formed during an animal's first encounter with a novel environment and are subsequently replayed during off-line states to support consolidation and future behaviour.
evidence: This is background knowledge about hippocampal function stated in the abstract.
